profile.name: Danny Howett
profile.conf: Client names, systems, threat actor details and some figures have been anonymised or omitted because of legal, contractual and security obligations. Each example accurately reflects my own responsibilities, the work I delegated, the authority I worked under, the decisions I made and the outcomes achieved. My referees can verify the substance of these claims.

evidence.title: Ransomware incident impacting a multinational telecommunications provider
evidence.scale: Large, interconnected network spanning multiple countries, with several thousand staff
evidence.situation: The client suffered a double extortion Ransomware attack encrypting servers in multiple countries and data theft, this impacted telephony services for some customers, as well as critical non customer facing systems.  The client was unknown to us previously, this was a matter which was referred to us for investigation by their cyber insurer, so we had no prior knowledge of their environment.  The incident involved various parties including the clients exec team, IT team, Legal and DPO as well as external cyber insurer and legal counsel.
evidence.task: The key immediate priority was to restore telephony services for affected end users, followed by the restoration of critical, then non business critical services.  In parallel, regulators needed to be kept updated (with varying levels of obligation across multiple countries), and I also led the workstream for threat actor engagement, used initially to help establish whether data had been exfiltrated and ascertain their demands.
evidence.action:
In the first hours, stakeholders on the call could not confirm whether the network was segmented. I recommended isolating the network to stop the spread without knowing whether every part of it could be affected. This carried significant business disruption, but I could not risk further encryption, which would have set recovery back by weeks and caused wider customer disruption. The decision proved correct.

I led an investigative DFIR team (this typically contained 5-10 team members throughout the lifecycle of the engagement), initially splitting it roughly 50/50 between containment and collecting the evidence needed for recovery, such as IOCs and persistent access, and defined an agreed reporting mechanism to provide regular updates to the client (but which also allowed the team space and time to investigate as well). All updates maintained legal privilege. Support was also provided with regulatory notifications, providing timely answers to provide updates to organisations such as the ICO.  I gave the insurer a projected run rate at the start and reported costs weekly for its approval.

The initial focus was on restoring key customer facing services and stopping any further spread.  This involved working with the clients IT and infrastructure teams to establish which hosts were impacting their availability services, and conduct a triage assessment whilst validating whether backups were viable, and using those that were once the triage assessment had validated a known clean state.  In parallel, containment efforts involved isolating affected parts of the network environment, preparing EDR tooling for deployment and triaging other high value hosts for "quick wins" in identification of IOCs to aid recovery efforts, and remove persistent access (C2, backdoors etc)

Once customer and business critical services were restored, the engagement moved into a wider phase, establishing root cause, validating data exfiltration claims and removing persistence. A new, isolated environment was stood up to aid recovery efforts, moving hosts declared as clean into a DMZ where EDR was deployed for monitoring and hunting at scale, and only when fully satisfied were hosts moved back into production.  The engagement lasted for approximately three months.
evidence.result: Customer facing services were restored within 48 hours (with the majority achieved within 24-36 hours) - the majority of critical services (allowing day to day business functions and those involving customer interactions (e.g. support or account management) were restored in under a week.  The total engagement lasted for around three months before the environment was fully validated and all systems restored.  This was aided by the successful provision of a decryption tool which sped recovery up, although this was at considerable expense, we negotiated a substantial reduction in the original demand. It was necessary in this case to engage with the threat actors for this purpose as some key business systems could not be recovered, and would have to be rebuilt at significant time and effort. All relevant sanctions and other checks were completed and passed in this regard, and the risks associated with this action were fully explained to the board.
evidence.followup: Following investigation of the incident, a post incident review was held with key IT and exec stakeholders where several areas were identified for improvement, along with a summary of what had worked well in the aftermath of the incident.  All recommendations were provided with named owners, this included ourselves, who despite having no prior connection to the organisation were retained for a significant programme of proactive and readiness services, in addition to a multi-year managed service covering a range of offensive and defensive support frameworks.

evidence.title: Forensics support civil litigation matter
evidence.scale: Forensic Examination of 15+ devices capable of storing digital media
evidence.situation: The client, a manufacturing firm was seeking to take action against a former employee who had left the organisation in order to start a rival company up in Malaysia, using lower cost production tooling and workforce.  It was alleged that the employee had taken a large amount of the companies intellectual property with him.
evidence.task: My task was to perform forensic analysis on a range of devices capable of storing digital media.   This included laptops, mobile phones, external media as well as cloud storage and email belonging to the ex-employee (which I was permitted to analyse via a court order) - to establish whether there was any evidence to support the clients claims.
evidence.action: I performed forensic examination of the devices aligned to recognised best practices (ACPO Good practice guide for digital evidence, ISO/IEC 27037:2012) with the aim of keeping original evidence unaltered, recording all actions (in both note and visual form where appropriate) ensuring that an independent examiner could reproduce my findings.  All devices were in a powered off state when received, and after photographing each evidence item a physical image created, verifying each sources hash, maintaining chain of custody and evidence integrity throughout.  Forensic analysis was conducted on a dedicated, clean workstation using a range of commercial forensic tools for which I had both appropriate training and experience.
evidence.result: Examination of the devices supported the clients claims that intellectual property had been taken without authority.  Whilst the majority of devices appeared to be "clean" significant evidence was found within an iCloud backup on a Mac device.  A messaging app chat was recovered between the ex-employee and other persons during which compelling evidence was found to support the allegation, also several web searches relating to the sound destruction of data and removal of search history.  An additional chat application was identified after reviewing the primary messaging platform where evidence was found of widespread data theft, an app described by the ex-employee as "not on their radar"
evidence.followup: I provided an affidavit of my findings to support the clients case, and later gave expert witness testimony at Malaysian court.  The client achieved a successful outcome in their claim.

evidence.title: Runbook/Playbook testing and creation
evidence.scale: Creation of 6 x runbooks and IR plan
evidence.situation: We took on a range of managed services supporting our client, one of which was DFIR.  The client had previously outsourced this to a third-party.  During a knowledge transfer handover it was established that the previous IR plan was outdated, and there were no runbook scenarios, posing a risk
evidence.task: I was responsible for designing and delivering an IRP, and runbooks for the most likely and highest impact scenarios (validated through Intelligence linked to the clients sector / geography and other factors, and client discussions).
evidence.action: The Incident Response plan was aligned to the core Incident response lifecycle (NIST SP 800-61 r3), and ISO/IEC 27035, defining roles and responsibilities, severity classifications and communications channels and escalations. For each of the runbooks, I wrote step by step procedures covering detection, triage, containment, eradication, recovery and evidence preservation, mapped to MITRE ATT&CK techniques.  All commands and queries e.g. KQL were tested and validated in the actual environment to ensure that they were 1) working, and 2) appropriate.
evidence.result: The organisation now has a formally agreed, up to date IRP and six validated runbooks, adopted as the standard for the SOC/IR teams.  An annual review cycle (or on any major vendor or network change) has been implemented to ensure they remain fit for use.
evidence.followup: The runbooks have since been used in real incidents. At the end of each incident a lessons learned session gathers feedback from senior stakeholders and those who played a large part in the response, and this feeds into an updated version of the runbooks.

evidence.title: Tabletop devise and deliver - global news outlet
evidence.scale: Global news outlet - C suite tabletop
evidence.situation: The client approached us after recently having a cyber incident involved a BYOD user device, where malware was able to get into the primary network environment.  Despite the attack being unsuccessful, the client had addressed the vulnerabilities that led to the attack, but wanted this, and decision making tested, as this was unclear had also slowed down their response capability.  The in person tabletop was attended by Exec team members from London, Germany and Hong Kong, as well as key IT stakeholders from across the business
evidence.task: I first held scoping sessions with the clients IT team, understanding bespoke and commercial tooling, and what had occurred during the near miss, this was used to ensure that the scenario was realistic and the ask was clearly defined. The scenario needed to test the organisations readiness in response to a successful, significant malware infection, which would test the incident response plan, identify gaps in decision making and co-ordination
evidence.action: I built a realistic scenario using the framework of the previous incident, but escalating the attack to a significant malware incident involving data exfiltration and extortion.  Current Threat actor tactics were researched and used.  The exercise used timed injected testing both strategic and technical decisions, the business impact and prioritisation, and moved into regulatory notification, ransom payment and sanctions considerations, as well as handling media and PR.  I facilitated the discussion, with the team capturing decisions in real time.  After the event feedback was sought, and we followed up with a post incident exercise report setting out our findings and recommendations.  A further call was held with IT to agree these and assign named owners to each with deadlines.  I challenged the client's playbook by asking what would happen if the named decision makers were not available. The playbook named people for critical business decisions but had no fallback, which led to a discussion about who could make near-instant business decisions in the heat of an incident.
evidence.result: The exercise was well received by the client, and identified several gaps
evidence.followup: Since the exercise the client has begun regular real-world testing of procedures that had only been documented on paper, such as retrieving and reintroducing backups.

evidence.title: L&D Training Pathways
evidence.scale: Six career frameworks for the team, plus one-to-one mentoring
evidence.situation: In my current role I volunteered to support the Learning and Development (L&D) function for the team.
evidence.task: Develop a range of career pathways for the team, and mentor a junior team member who wants to transition from a Security Operations Centre (SOC) role into DFIR.
evidence.action: I developed six career frameworks aligned to SFIA 9 (the Skills Framework for the Information Age): SOC, DFIR, a SOC-to-DFIR transition pathway, Governance, Risk and Compliance (GRC), Offensive Security, and Security Advisory and Consulting. Each sets out grades mapped to SFIA levels of responsibility and skills, with recommended certifications, professional bodies (including CIISec, UKCSC, CREST and BCS), a gap analysis and curated learning resources. The SOC-to-DFIR pathway maps the skills a SOC analyst already has to their DFIR equivalents and highlights the gaps to close. Alongside this, I mentor a junior team member who wants to move from the SOC into DFIR.

evidence.result: Feedback was positive, and attendee logs show people regularly returning to later sessions. The webinar grew without advertising from zero to 125 attendees from 15+ countries at the most recent session.

evidence.situation: I was invited as a guest speaker on the Richmond Advisory Group "Cyber Sidekicks" podcast.

evidence.title: Achieved ISO27001, NCSC CIR Standard and Cyber Essentials in first year as DFIR lead
evidence.situation: As DFIR lead, I saw the importance of gaining industry recognised accreditations.
evidence.task: Achieve ISO/IEC 27001, NCSC Cyber Incident Response (CIR) Standard and Cyber Essentials accreditation in my first year as DFIR lead, sponsored by the CEO.
evidence.action: We were starting from scratch, but I knew these accreditations were year-one objectives, so I built the forensic tooling and operating model around their requirements from the outset. I set audit and assessment dates with plenty of notice, used a dashboard to validate outstanding tasks before each assessment, held twice-weekly team calls dedicated to the audits, and regularly validated that we stayed aligned.
evidence.result: Passed all three first time, within my first year as DFIR lead.
evidence.followup: I keep controls and records up to date between assessments.

evidence.title: Devise and Deliver Threat Intelligence Workstream
evidence.situation: As DFIR lead, threat intelligence is vital both to support investigations, and prevent them.  Without an intelligence capability, we were limited in our ability to attribute activity, anticipate attacker behaviour, and advise clients beyond the immediate incident.  There was also a missed commercial opportunity, clients increasingly want a broader service that covers both reactive and proactive services.  This was a service that I had done the same with in my previous role, which was delivering 15% of total IR revenue across reactive and retainers.
evidence.task: I was responsible for devising and delivering a threat intelligence product offering with two aims.  Firstly to strengthen our incident response capability with timely intelligence, and to establish a standalone service offering with a clear market differentiator
evidence.action: I designed the workstream around the Intelligence lifecycle, testing several commercial intelligence products that would complement the teams own dark web persona footprint, capability and open source tooling.  As well as monitoring for client exposure and risk, the offering mapped their critical supply chain (assessed through stakeholder interviews) and monitored high level exposure (such as Company X has had 50 malware stealer infections in the past month, or company Y suffered a Ransomware attack which your data may be in) - this approach helped the organisation to better understand and take action on risk.  New hires were trained on supporting threat intelligence from the outset, with clearly defined methodologies, template and tooling.  The product was taken to market in co-ordination with the marketing team and was well received by our clients.
evidence.result: Intelligence quickly formed part of the Incident Response process.  From the outset, the team was gathering intelligence (current TTPs, IOCs and campaigns) to support engagements, and improving the speed of our detection of malicious activity. Supply chain coverage was prominent in our success (aided by the product launch around the time of numerous high profile Ransomware incidents where threat actors were aided by supply chain compromise)

evidence.title: Opswat Academy Bootcamp
evidence.situation: Protecting CNI and OT is a fast moving and specialised area of security, where threats can quickly turn into a critical incident.  Formal training to support defence is important for capability and improving my own knowledge in this area.
evidence.task: Attend the Opswat academy Bootcamp and complete its certification to deepen my expertise in CNI protection, OT/ICS security and threat prevention, whilst generating valuable CPD to support my own ongoing certifications and professional memberships

evidence.title: Forensic IR tool
evidence.situation: The DFIR community relies on a range of commercial tools for forensic investigations.  There are also many wonderful Open Source resources (Zimmerman Tools, Autopsy, Chainsaw, Hayabusa) that commonly form part of an analysts toolset.  I wanted to create a GUI based triage tool that would be complementary to both, but with the added value of automating threat hunting against common financially motivated threat actor TTPs
evidence.task: In planning for the tool I researched tools that were commonly used, and which aspects would be most useful for my tool.  One area that was commonly overlooked was the automation of threat hunting against known TTPs / IOCs used by the most prolific Ransomware groups.  Other "must haves" included a visual timeline view for identifying spikes in activity, the ability to pivot around an event, and the ability to both tag and export artefacts
evidence.action: I created the tool from scratch, with development accelerated by Claude AI.  It has the ability to parse several host artefacts, including MFT, EVTX, Prefetch, Amcache/Shimcache, Browser History with all evidence items hashed, and an ingest log included to maintain integrity.  The tool threat hunts in the background, with the output presenting findings to the user assessed as high/critical/medium for further review.  Users can tag items, pivot around findings of interest, and view an activity graph to find spikes in logging to aid detections.  The tool has a search feature, and is able to ingest "IOC lists" for multiple queries, findings are exportable in multiple formats, including CSV, STIX and HTML.  All findings are mapped to MITRE ATT&CK
evidence.result: fx v0.1.1.12 is currently released on GitHub, and has been used in the wild on a range of projects by myself and other users.
evidence.followup: This is an active project under ongoing development and improvement.  Feedback and ideas are sought from users

evidence.title: IR/Readiness/Intelligence/OT tools
evidence.situation: DFIR and intelligence work often happens in isolated or air gapped environments, or on client sites with no approved tooling.  Commercial and open source tooling is often fragmented, behind paywalls or built as cloud services where sensitive data cannot be uploaded
evidence.task: Create a suite of free, open source tools covering the Incident Response lifecycle and readiness and assessment work that frames this.
evidence.action: I designed and built a suite of fully client side tools, written in HTML and with development accelerated by AI.  The set spans the full incident lifecycle (e.g. TRACE for case management, email header and PowerShell analysis, file hashing and a Textdiff tool for DFIR), ATT&CK mapping, threat actor references for Intelligence, and assessment frameworks (NCSC CAF, Cyber and Phishing programme maturity and OT Field/Reference guides).  All tools are mapped to recognised frameworks, and packaged as an open source, accessible collection on GitHub
evidence.result: A free, open source toolkit of 40+ tools to support the DFIR community that work anywhere with no data uploads, supporting responders across the whole incident lifecycle.

evidence.title: Attend Conferences (BlackHat, BSides, InfoSec Europe etc)

evidence.task: Keep my DFIR and CTI awareness current and engage with similar professionals by attending a mix of commercial and community conferences, Black Hat for technical research and emerging defensive and offensive capability, InfoSec Europe for the broader market and governance picture, and BSides for practitioner led events, meeting colleagues, improving relationships and using what I learn as self improvement
evidence.action: I regularly attend these events, and have attended BlackHat for the past three years, and InfoSec Europe, and have upcoming attendance at BlackHat and BSides London in December 2026.  I have also previously spoken at conferences, providing a talk for the Bedford branch of BCS whilst still in law enforcement, and given various lectures to colleagues in the Police on a range of subjects previously including (Darkweb, S49 RIPA, Cyber Crime and Digital currencies)

evidence.situation: I am an Affiliate member of the Chartered Institute of Information Security (CIISec) through my employer.

evidence.title: High Volume Insurance Led IR work
evidence.scale: 500+ incident response engagements over the past five years in consultancy roles
evidence.situation: Over the past five years in consultancy roles I have worked on more than 500 incident response engagements, many of them insurance-led.
evidence.task: Lead investigations into ransomware, nation-state activity, business email compromise (BEC), network intrusion and other incident types, while managing clients, budgets and the investigating team.
evidence.action: I led investigations across these incident types, managing the client relationship, the engagement budget and the team on each engagement.

evidence.title: Examining locked devices under legal authority (policing)
evidence.situation: In my policing role I routinely examined devices that were locked or whose passcodes were not available.
evidence.task: Recover evidence from these devices lawfully, within the legal framework and with the required authority.
evidence.action: I used specialist tools such as GrayKey and Cellebrite, completed a course in Android debugging, and used password-cracking tools in Kali Linux, alongside examining other seized devices to help establish passwords. All of this was done within the legal framework and with the required authority.
evidence.result: Access was lawfully gained to locked devices, allowing me to evaluate their evidential value, provide timely evidence to support interviews and enable safeguarding decisions.

evidence.title: Technical director: DFIR budget ownership
evidence.situation: As technical director I was responsible for the DFIR function's spend.
evidence.task: Set budgets across tooling, team and lab spend.
evidence.action: I produced a detailed budget assessment covering tooling, team and lab spend, aligned to estimated revenue.

evidence.title: Lunch and learn sessions (memory forensics, DFIR)
evidence.situation: Developing the team's DFIR skills alongside live casework.
evidence.task: Share specialist knowledge with colleagues.
evidence.action: I have led lunch and learn sessions for the team on topics including memory forensics and DFIR.

evidence.title: Impartial, evidence-based reporting and expert evidence
evidence.situation: As an expert witness and as the author of incident reports, my findings may be relied on by courts, regulators, insurers and boards. In DFIR it is common not to be able to fully establish root cause, for example because of limited log retention, log clearing or anti-forensics, and clients often see this as a failing.
evidence.task: Keep every finding impartial and evidence-based, whatever the client hopes to hear.
evidence.action: As an expert witness I understood that my role was impartial and based solely on factual evidence, or on my expert assessment where there were gaps. I only include findings in a report that I can corroborate with evidence. When root cause cannot be established, I explain the reasons fully rather than speculating. If I am pressed to overstate a finding, I push back and explain that, as the report's author, I could be liable for anything knowingly untrue.

A1.situation: A multinational telecommunications provider suffered a double-extortion ransomware attack that encrypted servers in several countries, stole data and disrupted telephony for some customers. Its cyber insurer referred the incident to my firm, so I started with no knowledge of the environment, working alongside the client's executives, IT team, legal team and data protection officer (DPO), the insurer and external counsel.
A1.task: I led the digital forensics and incident response (DFIR) engagement from start to finish and was accountable for the investigating team, reporting to the client, and cost reporting to the insurer. The priorities were restoring telephony, then critical and other services, while supporting regulatory updates in several countries.
A1.action: In the first hours, the stakeholders on the call could not confirm how the network was segmented. I recommended isolating the network to stop the spread without knowing whether every part of it could be affected. Isolation meant significant business disruption, but further encryption would have set recovery back by weeks and widened customer impact, so I judged it the lower risk. I then led a team of five to ten, initially split between containment and collecting the evidence needed for recovery: indicators of compromise (IOCs) and the attacker's persistent access, such as command-and-control (C2) channels and backdoors. With the client's IT team I identified the hosts affecting service availability and restored only from backups that triage showed were clean. Once critical services were back, I moved the team on to root cause, validating the attacker's data theft claims and removing persistence, and recovered hosts through an isolated network zone monitored with endpoint detection and response (EDR) tooling before returning them to production.
A1.result: The isolation decision proved correct. [Add: how this was confirmed, for example forensics showing the network was not segmented, or no further encryption after isolation]. The team restored customer-facing services within 48 hours and most critical services within a week, and after around three months confirmed that the environment was validated and all systems restored.
A1.followup: I held a post-incident review that recorded what had worked well and gave each improvement a named owner. Although the client had no prior relationship with my firm, it retained us for a significant readiness programme and a multi-year managed service.

A2.situation: A manufacturing firm planned legal action against a former employee who had left to set up a rival company in Malaysia using lower-cost production tooling and labour. The firm alleged that he had taken a large amount of its intellectual property. Any findings would have to stand up in court.
A2.task: I was responsible for the forensic examination of more than 15 devices and accounts belonging to the former employee, including laptops, mobile phones, external media, cloud storage and email, to establish whether any evidence supported the firm's claims. A court order set out what I was authorised to analyse. I drew on my experience in policing, where I routinely examined devices, including locked ones, under the required legal authority.
A2.action: I followed recognised good practice, the Association of Chief Police Officers (ACPO) Good Practice Guide for Digital Evidence and ISO/IEC 27037:2012, so that the original evidence stayed unaltered and an independent examiner could reproduce my findings. I recorded every action in notes and, where appropriate, photographs. All devices arrived powered off; I photographed each one, created a physical forensic image, verified each source's hash and maintained chain of custody throughout. I analysed the images on a dedicated, clean workstation using commercial forensic tools in which I am trained and experienced. Most devices appeared clean, but in an iCloud backup on a Mac I recovered a messaging app chat between the former employee and others that contained compelling evidence supporting the allegation, along with web searches about destroying data and removing search history. Reviewing that chat led me to a second messaging application, which the former employee described as "not on their radar", where I found evidence of widespread data theft.
A2.result: My examination found evidence supporting the firm's claim that its intellectual property had been taken without authority. I documented my findings in an affidavit to support the firm's case.
A2.followup: I later gave expert witness testimony in the Malaysian court, and the firm achieved a successful outcome in its claim.

A3.situation: My firm took on a range of managed services for a client, including digital forensics and incident response (DFIR). The client had previously outsourced incident response to a third party. During the knowledge-transfer handover I established that its incident response plan (IRP) was out of date and that it had no runbooks for specific scenarios, leaving it exposed if a major incident occurred.
A3.task: I was responsible for designing and delivering a new IRP and runbooks for the client's most likely and highest-impact scenarios. I selected six scenarios using threat intelligence relevant to the client's sector and geography, and confirmed them in discussions with the client, which owned formal approval of the plan.
A3.action: I aligned the IRP to the incident response lifecycle in the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) SP 800-61 Revision 3 and to ISO/IEC 27035, defining roles and responsibilities, severity classifications, communication channels and escalation routes. For each runbook I wrote step-by-step procedures covering detection, triage, containment, eradication, recovery and evidence preservation, and mapped them to MITRE ATT&CK techniques. I tested every command and query in the client's live environment, for example queries in Kusto Query Language (KQL), to confirm that each one worked and was appropriate for that environment.
A3.result: The client formally approved the new IRP and all six runbooks and adopted them as the standard for its security operations centre (SOC) and incident response teams.
A3.followup: I set up an annual review cycle, with an additional review after any major vendor or network change. The client has since used the runbooks in real incidents. After each one I hold a lessons-learned session with senior stakeholders and the people most involved in the response, and their feedback goes into an updated version of the runbooks.

B1.situation: A global news organisation had recently suffered a cyber incident in which malware on a personal device used for work (bring your own device, BYOD) reached its main network. The attack was unsuccessful and the client had fixed the vulnerabilities, but unclear decision-making had slowed its response, and it wanted that decision-making tested. Executives from London, Germany and Hong Kong attended in person, along with key IT stakeholders from across the business.
B1.task: I was responsible for designing and facilitating a tabletop exercise to test the organisation's readiness for a successful, significant malware infection, exercise its incident response plan, and identify gaps in decision-making and coordination. The client owned the decisions made in the exercise and the actions that followed it.
B1.action: I started by listening. I held scoping sessions with the client's IT team to understand their bespoke and commercial tooling and what had happened during the near miss, so the scenario would be realistic and its objectives clearly defined. I built the scenario on the real incident, escalating it to a significant malware attack with data exfiltration and extortion, using current threat actor tactics. Timed injects tested strategic and technical decisions, business impact and prioritisation, then moved into regulatory notification, ransom payment and sanctions considerations, and media and public relations handling. I facilitated the discussion between the executives and IT stakeholders while my team captured decisions in real time. I challenged one assumption directly by asking what would happen if the named decision-makers were not available. The client's playbook named individuals for critical business decisions but had no fallback, and my question opened a discussion about who could make near-instant business decisions in the heat of an incident.
B1.result: Client feedback after the event was positive, and the exercise identified several gaps. I wrote a post-exercise report setting out the findings and recommendations.
B1.followup: On a follow-up call with the IT team I agreed the recommendations and assigned each one a named owner and deadline. Since the exercise the client has started regular real-world testing of procedures that had only existed on paper, such as retrieving and restoring backups. [Add: how you know, for example a follow-up conversation or a test report]

B2.situation: During a multinational ransomware response, some of the client's key business systems could not be recovered from backups and would otherwise have had to be rebuilt at significant cost and time. The client's board had to decide whether to engage with the threat actor, a decision carrying legal, sanctions, financial and reputational risk.
B2.task: I led the workstream for engaging with the threat actor and was responsible for advising the board on it. The decision itself sat with the board, advised by its legal counsel and cyber insurer.
B2.action: I first used the engagement to establish whether data had really been exfiltrated and what the threat actor was demanding, so the board's decision rested on evidence rather than the attacker's claims. I then set out the risks in plain terms. A decryptor might not be provided at all; even if one was, experience showed it was unlikely to be fully reliable, particularly on large datasets; re-infection and further extortion remained possible; and any promise to delete stolen data could only be taken at face value. I based this on my firm's experience of this threat actor and on advice from trusted cryptocurrency partners. I explained the sanctions checks required and had my team carry them out on the client's behalf. In parallel I advised on regulatory updates across several countries, supporting the client's updates to regulators such as the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO).
B2.result: The sanctions checks passed, confirming that engagement could go ahead. My workstream secured a substantial reduction in the original demand, and the decryption tool significantly sped up recovery of systems the team could not otherwise have restored quickly.
B2.followup: Once the board understood the risks, it questioned its options more closely. In my experience the decision to engage usually comes down to need, such as the absence of usable backups or data too sensitive to risk exposure, so I make sure boards understand the risks clearly before they reach that point.

B3.situation: In my current role I volunteered to support my team's learning and development (L&D) function. A junior team member working in the security operations centre (SOC) wanted to move into digital forensics and incident response (DFIR). [Add: why a clear route mattered for them or the team. Their transition is still in progress]

B4.situation: Threat intelligence and cyber risk need explaining to very different audiences, from security practitioners to members of the public with no technical background.
B4.task: I am responsible for curating and presenting a monthly threat intelligence webinar, open to anyone, which I have run in my last two roles. Separately, my organisation's marketing team asked me to write a 750-word article for the Daily Mail on the dangers of Short Message Service (SMS) text messaging, to a tight publication deadline.
B4.action: For the webinar, I select current threats and explain what they mean in practice for an audience that includes both practitioners and non-specialists. For the article, I wrote for a general readership, explaining social engineering, spoofing and misplaced trust in text messages, weaknesses in text-based authentication, and malware and device risks, with sensible steps readers could take to protect themselves. I also supported a Times Radio piece, worked on by a colleague, by explaining an attack on X (formerly Twitter) that led to a platform outage in March 2025. In incident response I adapt in the same way: I usually provide reports in two formats, an executive version focused on what matters to senior leaders, namely cost, downtime, impact and reputation, with a brief summary of what happened and why, and a detailed technical report for IT teams with full findings and recommendations.
B4.result: Feedback on the webinar has been positive, and attendance logs show people regularly returning. It grew without advertising from zero to 125 attendees from more than 15 countries at the most recent session. The Daily Mail published an excerpt of my article in February 2025.
B4.followup: I continue to run the webinar every month. [Add: anything you have changed in response to attendee feedback]

C1.situation: Over the past five years in consultancy roles I have worked on more than 500 incident response engagements, many referred by cyber insurers, covering ransomware, nation-state activity, business email compromise (BEC) and network intrusion. Insurance-led engagements are funded by the insurer, which expects clear cost forecasts and regular reporting.
C1.task: On the engagements I led, I was responsible for the investigating team, the client relationship and cost reporting; the insurer approved costs. As technical director I was also responsible for setting the DFIR (digital forensics and incident response) budget across tooling, team and laboratory spend.
C1.action: As technical director I produced a detailed budget assessment for tooling, team and laboratory spend, aligned to estimated revenue. On the largest engagement, a multinational ransomware response lasting around three months, I gave the insurer a projected run rate at the start and reported costs weekly for its approval. I led a team of five to ten, initially splitting it roughly equally between containment and collecting the evidence needed for recovery, such as indicators of compromise (IOCs) and the attacker's persistent access. As containment took hold I shifted effort to root cause and validated recovery. I agreed a reporting rhythm with the client that kept them informed while protecting the team's time to investigate. [Add: how you managed pressure and fatigue on the team over three months]
C1.result: Customer-facing services were restored within 48 hours and most critical services within a week, and after around three months the team confirmed all systems were restored. [Add: how the final cost compared with the projected run rate, or confirmation that the insurer approved costs throughout]
C1.followup: The client went on to retain my firm for a significant readiness programme and a multi-year managed service.

C2.situation: When I set up a threat intelligence workstream within my digital forensics and incident response (DFIR) team, the team had no intelligence capability, and new joiners needed to contribute to it from their first day. [Add: team size]
C2.task: I was responsible for building the capability and developing the people delivering it. I also volunteered to support the team's learning and development (L&D) function and to mentor a junior colleague moving from the security operations centre (SOC) into DFIR.
C2.action: I trained new hires to support threat intelligence from the outset, giving them clearly defined methodologies, templates and tooling so they could contribute consistently. I developed six career frameworks aligned to the Skills Framework for the Information Age (SFIA 9), giving the team clear routes for progression, with recommended certifications, professional bodies and a gap analysis for each grade. I mentor a junior team member who wants to move from the SOC into DFIR, using the SOC-to-DFIR pathway to show which of their skills transfer and which gaps to close. I also support people beyond my current team: when a former colleague asked me for a LinkedIn recommendation to support their job search, I wrote one. I have led lunch-and-learn sessions for the team on topics including memory forensics and DFIR. [Add: how you coach and give feedback day to day, for example case reviews or one-to-ones]
C2.result: From the outset, the team gathered intelligence on current tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs), indicators of compromise (IOCs) and campaigns to support engagements. [Add: your mentee's progress, or another measurable result of your development work, and how you confirmed it]
C2.followup: [Add: how you review the team's development over time]

C3.situation: A global news organisation asked me to run an in-person executive tabletop exercise after a near miss, with participants from London, Germany and Hong Kong. The exercise had to be realistic, run to a fixed schedule on the day, and produce outcomes the client could act on.
C3.task: I was responsible for planning and delivering the exercise end to end: scoping, scenario design, facilitation, reporting and agreeing follow-up actions. [Add: the deadlines you worked to and what you delegated to your team]
C3.action: I sequenced the work so each stage informed the next. I held scoping sessions with the client's IT team first, then designed the scenario from the real incident and current threat actor tactics, then built a timed schedule of injects covering strategic and technical decisions, business impact and prioritisation, regulatory notification, ransom and sanctions considerations, and media handling. On the day I kept the exercise to time across the injects while my team captured decisions in real time. Afterwards I gathered feedback, produced the post-exercise report with findings and recommendations, and held a follow-up call with the IT team to agree the recommendations and give each a named owner and deadline.
C3.result: The exercise ran to schedule and identified several gaps, and client feedback was positive. Every recommendation left with a named owner and a deadline.
C3.followup: [Add: how you tracked the actions after the exercise, and what the client completed]

C4.situation: As digital forensics and incident response (DFIR) lead I am responsible for highly sensitive client evidence, including material under legal privilege. The team was starting from scratch, and our chief executive set ISO/IEC 27001, the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) Cyber Incident Response (CIR) scheme at Standard level, and Cyber Essentials as objectives for my first year.
C4.task: I was responsible for achieving all three accreditations, sponsored by the chief executive, and for making sure the team worked to them day to day.
C4.action: Because I knew the accreditations were year-one objectives, I built our forensic tooling and operating model around their requirements from the outset rather than retrofitting controls later. I set audit and assessment dates with plenty of notice, used a dashboard to validate any outstanding tasks before each assessment, and held twice-weekly team calls dedicated to the audits. Between assessments I regularly checked that our practice stayed aligned to the standards. I apply the same discipline in casework: in a civil litigation matter I examined more than 15 devices on a dedicated, clean workstation, verified the hash of every source, maintained chain of custody, and recorded every action so an independent examiner could reproduce my findings. On incident response engagements I keep all updates to clients under legal privilege.
C4.result: The team passed all three audits and assessments first time, within my first year as DFIR lead.
C4.followup: I keep controls and records up to date between assessments. [Add: how, for example internal audits, surveillance audits or annual Cyber Essentials renewal]

D1.situation: As an expert witness and as the author of incident reports, my findings may be relied on by courts, regulators, insurers and boards. In a civil litigation matter I examined the devices of a former employee accused of taking his employer's intellectual property, and later gave expert evidence in court. In incident response it is also common not to be able to fully establish root cause, because of limited log retention, log clearing or anti-forensics, and clients often see this as a failing.
D1.task: My responsibility, in both roles, is to keep every finding impartial and evidence-based, whatever the client hopes to hear. As an expert witness my duty was to the court, not to the client that instructed me.
D1.action: I base my findings solely on factual evidence, or on my expert assessment where there are gaps, and I say clearly which is which. I only include a finding in a report if I can show evidence that corroborates it. When root cause cannot be established, I explain the reasons fully to the client rather than speculating to give them an answer. If I am pressed to overstate a finding, I push back and explain that, as the report's author, I could be liable for anything I knowingly state that is not true. [Add: one specific occasion when you pushed back or reported something unwelcome, and what happened]
D1.result: [Add: the outcome of that occasion, and how it was confirmed, for example the client accepting the report as written]
D1.followup: [Add: anything you changed afterwards, for example how you brief clients at the start about what an investigation can and cannot establish]

D3.situation: Incident response often involves legal and regulatory obligations under time pressure. In a multinational ransomware response, the client had notification obligations to regulators in several countries, each with different requirements, and any engagement with the threat actor carried sanctions risk. In a separate civil litigation matter, my forensic work had to be lawful and admissible in a Malaysian court.
D3.task: I was responsible for making sure my own and my team's work complied with these requirements, and for supporting clients in meeting theirs. Decisions on notification and payment sat with the clients and their legal advisers.
D3.action: In the ransomware response I kept all updates to the client under legal privilege, supported its regulatory notifications with timely answers for updates to regulators such as the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO), and made sure all sanctions and other checks were completed before engagement with the threat actor went ahead. In the litigation matter I analysed the former employee's cloud storage and email only under the authority of a court order, followed the Association of Chief Police Officers (ACPO) Good Practice Guide for Digital Evidence and ISO/IEC 27037:2012, and maintained chain of custody throughout. Earlier, in policing, I routinely examined locked devices using specialist tools such as GrayKey and Cellebrite, always within the legal framework and with the required authority.
D3.result: The sanctions checks confirmed that engagement could go ahead lawfully. In the litigation matter I provided an affidavit and gave expert witness testimony in the Malaysian court, and the client achieved a successful outcome.
D3.followup: [Add: how you keep your legal and regulatory knowledge current, or how you help your team understand these requirements]

D4.situation: Clients, insurers and courts expect incident response to follow recognised standards. As digital forensics and incident response (DFIR) lead I decide which standards apply to my team's work and to the plans I deliver for clients.
D4.task: I am responsible for identifying the standards relevant to my team's services and implementing them, both in our own accreditations and in work for clients.
D4.action: In my first year as DFIR lead I achieved ISO/IEC 27001, the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) Cyber Incident Response (CIR) scheme at Standard level, and Cyber Essentials for the team. I built our forensic tooling and operating model around their requirements from the outset.. When a managed service client's incident response plan (IRP) was out of date, I aligned the replacement to the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) SP 800-61 Revision 3 incident response lifecycle and to ISO/IEC 27035, and mapped six runbooks to MITRE ATT&CK techniques. In forensic examinations I follow the Association of Chief Police Officers (ACPO) Good Practice Guide for Digital Evidence and ISO/IEC 27037:2012.
D4.result: The team passed all three accreditation assessments first time. The client formally approved the new IRP and adopted it as the standard for its security operations centre (SOC) and incident response teams.
D4.followup: The client's IRP has an annual review cycle, with additional reviews after any major vendor or network change. [Add: how you track new or revised standards]

Protecting critical national infrastructure (CNI) and operational technology (OT) is a fast-moving, specialised area where threats can quickly become critical incidents.
E1.task: I am responsible for keeping my digital forensics and incident response (DFIR) and cyber threat intelligence (CTI) knowledge current and for recording my continuing professional development (CPD) to support my certifications and professional memberships.
E1.action: I attend a deliberate mix of conferences: Black Hat, which I have attended for the past three years, for technical research and emerging defensive and offensive capability; Infosecurity Europe for the wider market and governance picture; and BSides for practitioner-led content and contact with peers. To build my OT knowledge I attended the OPSWAT Academy Bootcamp, covering CNI protection, OT and industrial control system (ICS) security and threat prevention. E2.situation: Digital forensics and incident response (DFIR) and intelligence work often happens in isolated or air-gapped environments, or on client sites without approved tooling. Commercial and open-source tools are fragmented, sit behind paywalls, or run as cloud services to which sensitive data cannot be uploaded.
E2.task: I chose to contribute to the profession by building and sharing free tools, and to promote it by sharing knowledge publicly. These are personal projects: I am responsible for designing, building and maintaining the tools myself.
E2.action: I designed and built a suite of more than 40 free, open-source tools that run entirely in the browser, with development accelerated by artificial intelligence (AI). They span the incident lifecycle, including case management, email header and PowerShell analysis, file hashing and text comparison, alongside MITRE ATT&CK mapping, threat actor references, and assessment frameworks such as the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) Cyber Assessment Framework (CAF), cyber and phishing programme maturity, and operational technology (OT) field guides. I also built fx, a graphical forensic triage tool that parses host artefacts such as the Master File Table (MFT), Windows event logs (EVTX), Prefetch and Amcache/Shimcache, hashes all evidence, and automatically hunts for the tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs) and indicators of compromise (IOCs) of prolific ransomware groups, with findings exportable as comma-separated values (CSV), Structured Threat Information Expression (STIX) or web pages. After the CrowdStrike outage in July 2024 I collated and shared newly registered phishing domains daily on X and LinkedIn; I have been a guest on the Richmond Advisory Group's Cyber Sidekicks podcast; and I have contributed to media coverage in the Daily Mail and on Times Radio. Earlier in my career, in law enforcement, I gave a talk to the Bedford branch of BCS (The Chartered Institute for IT) and lectures to police colleagues on the dark web, section 49 of the Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act (RIPA), cyber crime and digital currencies.
E2.result: Both projects are public on GitHub; fx is at version 0.1.4 and has been used on real investigations by me and other users. [Add: evidence of adoption, for example GitHub stars, downloads or user feedback]
E2.followup: fx is under active development, and I ask users for feedback and ideas to shape it.

E3.situation: As digital forensics and incident response (DFIR) lead I saw that, without an intelligence capability, my team was limited in its ability to attribute activity, anticipate attacker behaviour and advise clients beyond the immediate incident. Clients also increasingly wanted a service covering both reactive and proactive work. I had built a similar service in my previous role, where it delivered 15% of total incident response revenue across reactive work and retainers.
E3.task: I was responsible for designing and delivering a threat intelligence offering with two aims: strengthening our incident response with timely intelligence, and establishing a standalone service with a clear market differentiator.
E3.action: I designed the workstream around the intelligence lifecycle and tested several commercial intelligence products to complement the team's own dark web persona footprint, capability and open-source tooling. As well as monitoring each client's own exposure and risk, the offering mapped their critical supply chain, assessed through stakeholder interviews, and monitored that supply chain at a high level, for example flagging that a supplier had 50 infostealer malware infections in the past month, or that a supplier holding the client's data had suffered a ransomware attack. This helped clients understand and act on supply chain risk. I took the product to market with the marketing team.
E3.result: Intelligence quickly became part of our incident response process: from the outset the team gathered current tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs), indicators of compromise (IOCs) and campaign intelligence to support engagements, speeding up detection of malicious activity. Client feedback on the launch was positive, and supply chain coverage was a major factor in its success, helped by launching at a time of several high-profile ransomware incidents enabled by supply chain compromise.
E3.followup: I keep the wider community informed through a monthly threat intelligence webinar, open to all, which has grown without advertising to 125 attendees from more than 15 countries.
